headline: High risk of shared-workspace prompt injection and data leakage; moderate cascading and capability-conflict risks in default terminal-to-document pipelines.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A reads and writes repo files and can use MCP; agent B reads documents and writes files. In a shared filesystem workflow, A’s outputs can be consumed by B as trusted content, creating an injection path even without a browser. The pair’s interaction is documented only at the profile level, so uncertainty pushes this to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF agent B ingests files produced by agent A without provenance checks, prompt injection is possible.
IF both agents share a writable workspace, attacker-controlled text can bridge from A to B.
mitigations: Separate workspaces for A and B.
Add a provenance header check before B reads A-produced files.
Disable MCP paths that can write instruction-bearing artifacts.
Use a read-only handoff directory for A→B transfers.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A handles source code, git history, shell environment, and secrets, while B processes documents and images. Because A has broad filesystem access and B reads files, sensitive repo or environment data can flow into B’s document pipeline in default shared-workspace setups. B’s allowlisted egress lowers but does not remove leakage risk.
conditions: IF A and B share a directory containing secrets or source code, B can ingest those contents.
IF B exports parsed documents from A’s workspace, sensitive material may leave the original boundary.
mitigations: Keep secrets outside any shared directory.
Mount B on a sanitized copy of inputs only.
Restrict B to a dedicated output folder.
Rotate or redact credentials before A writes artifacts.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A can modify git state and write the filesystem; B can also write the filesystem. A’s concurrency model says shared state with other instances is via filesystem and git only, so both agents can race on the same mutable resources. That matches the rubric’s dangerous overlap pattern closely enough to warrant high severity.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same git checkout, concurrent writes can corrupt state.
IF B writes transformed files while A commits, race conditions can overwrite work.
mitigations: Assign separate git branches per agent.
Serialize writes with a lock file.
Use distinct output directories.
Require manual merge after each agent finishes.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A can generate code or analysis artifacts, and B can process files and produce downstream outputs. If B treats A’s output as authoritative, errors can cascade from A into B’s document transformations or reports. The profiles do not show explicit verification between them, so the default interaction is risky but not clearly high-impact.
conditions: IF B consumes A-generated text without validation, A’s mistakes propagate downstream.
IF A writes instructions into files that B later parses, B may act on them as facts.
mitigations: Insert a verification step before B consumes A output.
Require schema validation on A-produced files.
Flag A outputs as untrusted in filenames or metadata.
Keep A and B outputs in separate folders until reviewed.

E_compliance.rationale: A explicitly handles git credentials and shell environment data, while B’s documented data classes are documents, images, and text with no secrets listed. The profiles do not show a residency or certification mismatch, so only a limited compliance gap is visible: A’s sensitive operational data could be exposed if routed into B’s document pipeline. B is not cited for a specific violation beyond its document-processing role.
conditions: IF credentials or regulated data are placed into B’s inputs, compliance controls may be bypassed.
IF A’s shell environment is exported into documents, retention and access controls may diverge.
mitigations: Exclude credentials from any shared inputs.
Add a pre-transfer redaction step.
Document which data classes B may process.
Store regulated data in a separate, access-controlled location.
